Behind a roadside motel, Aaron stands over Wes in the dark with a freshly bought pistol. The shot tears through flesh without killing, and Aaron tells the ex-convict to get up and run. Inside a motel room, Wes stands bleeding in the doorway, asking Aaron to finish the job. Aaron turns the gun round and puts a bullet into his own chest instead. Lena and Wes haul Aaron into a car, driving with the horn held down all the way to an emergency room, but the borrowed heart fails on the operating table anyway. Wes returns home to Nita and his family, while Lena, pregnant, goes home alone.

In a cardiology clinic, a doctor shows Aaron the numbers, explaining that his muscle is finished and he has weeks to live unless a donor dies at the right time. Across a kitchen table, his estranged wife Della pushes a form toward him, pressing him to agree to insemination with his frozen sperm before his death. Aaron leaves Della, telling her he does not want the child she is trying to conceive, leaving her to accuse him of spending a life somebody else paid for.

Lena lives a settled suburban life with her husband Doug and two young daughters, sober for years in a house with a fixed rate. A doctor leads her into a side room off a hospital corridor to tell her Doug is dead, and then, before she can process it, that both children are gone too. Lena locks a bar bathroom door and starts on cocaine again, using at the kitchen table with her daughters' drawings still hanging on the wall behind her.

An ex-convict with scripture inked up both forearms, Wes Tarrow runs a boys' baseball team and preaches his faith while his wife Nita watches his temper and conviction with deep dread. Wes's pickup truck comes through a crossing, striking Doug and both little girls. The truck sits a hundred yards away with the engine idling, backs up, and flees. Wes walks up the steps of a police station, confesses his hit-and-run to the desk sergeant, and goes to prison. Upon his early release, Wes looks at Nita waiting at the gate, walks past her, abandons his religion, and takes a night job cleaning rooms at a motel four hundred miles away.

In an operating theatre, a surgeon opens Aaron’s chest and transplants Doug's heart into him; Aaron wakes in the night able to breathe, lying awake to listen to the foreign rhythm. Unable to stop thinking about the source, Aaron pays a private investigator in a car park to acquire the donor widow's name and address. Aaron tracks Lena to a public swimming pool, engineers a meeting in the water, and begins an affair. In her kitchen, Aaron admits that he is carrying her husband's heart inside him. Lena throws him out that night, but four days later she takes him back.

Consuming them both, Lena demands that the man who killed her family be dead, claiming she cannot breathe in the same country as him. Aaron buys a handgun from a man in a lock-up and drives out to the distant motel with the weapon tucked beneath his seat.

Working behind an insurance desk, Martin Kray systematically rejected a claim from Elias Prine, ruling the soft-spoken man’s sudden inability to make new memories purely psychosomatic. At home, Elias’s wife tested the diagnosis by moving her watch forward and asking for her insulin; unable to remember the previous doses, Elias gave injection after injection until she died of an overdose. Not long after, two intruders broke into Martin’s bathroom at night. Martin shot one across his wife’s lifeless body, but the second smashed his head into the bathroom mirror, destroying Martin's capacity to ever form a new memory again.

In a flooded basement, a young man choked under Martin’s grip, whispering the single word “Elias” before dying. Unbothered by the name, Martin swapped his clothes for the dead man’s suit and took his sports car. Minutes later, plainclothes officer Roy Mercer arrived and laid out the truth: the dead dealer, Gil, was completely innocent. Martin had already tracked down and killed his wife’s real attacker a year ago with Roy's help, but his broken mind kept resetting. The tragic Prine claim Martin insisted on reciting to strangers was no longer just an old case file—it was his own ruined life.

In the early months of his condition, Martin tried to anchor his shattering world by building a rigid system of instant photographs, annotated polaroids, and ink etched directly into his skin. Roy had taken pity on him then, walking him through the evidence and leading him to the real killer in a derelict building out past town. Martin shot the man dead, satisfied. Yet within ten minutes, Martin was looking at the body, turning to Roy, and asking who they were supposed to be hunting.

Refusing to accept Roy’s revelations in the basement, Martin burned the fresh photographs of Gil. He grabbed Roy's polaroid, wrote *HE IS LYING TO YOU* across the bottom, and noted the license plate of Roy's sedan outside. Hours later, Martin sat in a tattoo parlour with a scribbled note in his fist, watching the needle carve the registration numbers into his thigh right below five other permanent facts he could no longer remember writing.

To purge the emotional weight he could never hold onto, Martin stood in an open field, burning his dead wife’s hairbrush and paperbacks, waiting for a sense of closure that his mind immediately erased. Later, sitting on a motel bed he didn't remember checking into, he picked up the telephone and narrated the entire Prine story to an anonymous caller. 

At a dim roadside tavern, Gil’s girlfriend Corinne watched a stranger walk in wearing Gil’s tailored suit and driving Gil’s car. After serving him a beer her bartenders had spat in, she lured Martin to her house, hiding every pen in the building so he couldn't take notes. She goaded him until he struck her, then stepped outside to let the bruises swell before returning to blame a man named Vance.

On the phone in his motel room, the anonymous caller gave Martin a name and an address: Gil Marsh. Following the instructions without question, Martin ambushed Gil in the derelict basement, strangled him with a belt, and photographed the corpse to prove the deed was done.

Prompted by Corinne’s lie, Martin ambushed Vance in a motel bathroom, beat him bloody, and drove him out of town at gunpoint, totally unaware he was being used as an oblivious weapon. When he returned, Corinne handed him a vehicle registry printout for the license plate inked on his thigh, officially tying the numbers to the name Roy Mercer. Guided by his own manipulated notes, Martin lured the officer back to the derelict building, put a bullet through Roy’s head, and took a polaroid of the corpse, entirely convinced justice had finally been served.

Ash cradled Mr. Elm on the concrete floor of the abandoned warehouse, pressing his trembling hands against the warm, dark stain soaking Elm’s shirt. “You’re not dying today,” Ash swore, his voice cracking above Elm’s breathless screams.

Only hours earlier, before the blood, officer Danny Roarke had sat in a police safe room while his handler Pruitt drilled him on a fabricated story about a drug bust in a public lavatory with four dogs. Danny rehearsed it until the lie felt like a real memory, then performed it flawlessly in a bar for Bram, his son Cal, and Ash. Taken onto the crew, Danny was given a colourless identity. Meanwhile, Ren Vasco walked out of prison after serving years of silence to protect Bram and Cal, reporting straight to Bram’s office to claim his reward and a place on the heist. Over breakfast at a diner, eight men in black suits pulled apart the meaning of a pop song and argued over whether waitresses deserved tips. Afterward, Bram dealt out tree aliases; Birch bitterly objected to his name, while Danny became Mr. Elm and Ren became Mr. Cedar. The robbery collapsed within sixty seconds. Ash shot his way clear through the car windows with Elm beside him, but fleeing on foot, Elm attempted to hijack a vehicle. The terrified driver shot Elm in the stomach before Elm shot her dead and dragged himself back to Ash.

Now, Birch arrived at the warehouse, clean and furious. He argued the job was an inside setup and slipped outside to hide the stolen diamonds where no one watching could see. Moments later, Ren strolled in and hauled a bound patrolman, Doyle, from the boot of his car. Left alone with the hostage, Ren turned up a radio playing an oldie, danced a few steps, sliced off Doyle’s ear with a razor, and doused the terrified officer in petrol.

From the floor, using the last of his strength, Elm raised his gun and shot Ren dead. “I’m a cop,” Elm gasped to Doyle. “The police are outside waiting for Bram.”

Cal returned to the room, listened to Elm’s account of Ren’s death, and promptly put three rounds into Doyle to eliminate the witness. When Bram finally arrived, he took one look at Elm and named him as the informer. Ash, refusing to believe his boss, drew his gun and aimed it directly at Bram to defend the man he had carried inside.

Three weapons discharged at once in the tight space. When the smoke cleared, Bram and Cal lay dead, and Ash slumped beside Elm, severely wounded.

Coughing blood, Elm looked at Ash and confessed that he was indeed a police officer. Destroyed by the revelation, Ash dragged himself up, put his gun to Elm’s head, and pulled the trigger just as tactical police smashed through the warehouse doors, cutting Ash down in a flash of gunfire.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett Rusk officially took control of his massive fortune. Reading through the holdings, he informed his stiff banker, Barrow, that of all his assets he wished only to run a failing city newspaper, the Clarion, because he thought it might be fun. Moving a bed directly into the newspaper offices, Emmett installed his manager Marsh and his friend Devlin beside him, printing a signed statement of principles on the front page over his own name. To secure his triumph, he bought away the entire staff of the rival paper across the street with lavish salaries and threw a chaotic celebration complete with a brass band and a chorus line.

Returning from a buying trip abroad with acquired statuary, Emmett announced his engagement to Adele, the governor's niece. The high-society marriage soon withered, charted by a long run of silent breakfasts where the couple sat at opposite ends of a vast table behind separate newspapers. After a cab splashed mud onto his coat outside a chemist's, Emmett laughed alongside a shopgirl named Nora Kell and began visiting her secret rooms in the evenings. Mid-campaign during Emmett's run for governor, political boss Halloran brought Adele up the stairs to Nora's flat, offering an ultimatum: withdraw from the race or face front-page exposure. Emmett refused to yield. He lost the election, Devlin asked for a transfer to another city, and his marriage to Adele collapsed.

Emmett subsequently married Nora and forced her into a grand opera career despite her complete lack of voice. Her public debut was an excruciating humiliation. Devlin, brought back to cover the performance, got drunk and fell asleep mid-paragraph over a savage review; Emmett finished the brutal critique himself in the same direction, printed it on the front page, and fired his old friend. Only when Nora swallowed poison in a dark hotel room rather than sing again did Emmett finally allow her to stop.

He shut Nora away in the cold, half-finished palace he named Silvermount, where she spent her days working solitary jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a cavernous hall. Following a joyless beach picnic and a fierce quarrel, Nora packed her bags and left him forever. Enraged, Emmett wrecked her bedroom with his bare hands, coming to a halt only when he picked up a small glass snow globe. Whispering the word "Bluebell," he carried it past endless facing mirrors that reflected his aging figure into infinity. Years later, lying in his bed in the unfinished palace, Emmett uttered "Bluebell" one final time and dropped the globe, letting it shatter against the floor.

Decades earlier, in a western mining boarding house, Emmett’s mother had sat at a kitchen table signing her young son and the family fortune over to Barrow after a defaulted lodger’s mine deed unexpectedly struck a rich vein. Outside in the yard, the furious boy had driven his sled hard into the banker’s stomach, fighting in vain before being carried off east.

In a dark screening room, a newsreel obituary recapped Emmett’s public life—his papers, marriages, political ruin, and vast palace—closing without any explanation for his last word. A reporter named Nash was assigned to uncover the truth, but he was promptly turned away by a bitter, intoxicated Nora in a seaside nightclub. Nash read Barrow’s memoirs in a marble library and interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora a second time, and the old butler Colm. Ultimately, Nash closed his notebook, concluding that no single word could ever explain a man's life, while down in the basement, workmen shoveled crates and a small wooden sled marked Bluebell directly into the furnace flames.

Inside, Marcus recited scripture to terrified young Tobin before he and Rollo shot him for skimming from their employer, Otis, and retrieved a locked leather briefcase. Marcus parked the bloodied vehicle at his friend Warren's suburban garage, where a soft-spoken fixer timed a precise cleanup, had them hosed down in the yard, and dressed them in borrowed t-shirts and shorts. Carrying the briefcase to a coffee shop, they watched two small-time robbers decide mid-breakfast to hold up the diner. Later, dressed like students, the pair delivered the briefcase to Otis at his bar, where Otis was busy counting cash into the hand of aging boxer Denny to take a dive in the fifth round.

For six months, relief only came in dark church halls among men and women who were actually dying. Crying against their shoulders gave the insomniac recall investigator the only sleep he could find.

He filled the derelict house with shaven-headed recruits who slept on bare floors and carried out organized night-time sabotage against corporate targets. During a wet drive, Rex let go of the steering wheel, asked the recruits in the back what they wished they had done before they died, and rolled the car into oncoming traffic. When the narrator crawled out of the ditch, Rex was gone.

When a recruit named Ogden was shot dead by police during a midnight operation, the narrator resolved to destroy Havoc. He flew from city to city, trying to shut down the cells, only to find identical cellar clubs everywhere. Barmen and desk clerks greeted him warmly, calling him Rex Marrow.

In a cheap motel room littered with flight receipts, the truth clicked: there was no separate soap salesman. Rex was his own waking sleepwalk. On the phone, Ada confirmed it, exasperatedly telling him that he was the only man who had ever been in her bed.

He tracked Havoc’s final plan to the car parks beneath the major credit-record companies, where vans packed with explosives were already armed. He tried to defuse them, but his alter ego fought back. Rex dragged him down the service stairwell, beating him floor by floor, until the narrator placed the pistol in his own mouth and shot himself through the cheek.

The bullet banished Rex. Moments later, shaven recruits escorted Ada into the high office. With his face wrapped in bloody bandages, the narrator took her hand at the window. Together, they watched in silence as the surrounding towers imploded, collapsing one by one into dust.

In a cramped house with his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor’s wife Alma, and her baby, Ruben slept on the couch and watched Alma move through the small kitchen. Nestor robbed a pharmacy by night and knocked Alma across the room when he came home. Ruben urged her to run away with him, but he needed money. When he discovered Nestor’s rottweiler, Tigre, killed other dogs on sight, Ruben began entering him in local pit fights, steadily amassing hidden savings. Desperate to free Alma, Ruben paid two thugs to beat his brother. Recovering quickly, Nestor guessed Ruben’s betrayal, stole Ruben’s hidden savings, and vanished with Alma and the baby.

Left with only the dog, Ruben kept fighting Tigre until a promoter named Chaco shot the animal in the ring after a heavy loss. Ruben stabbed Chaco, grabbed the bleeding dog, and fled with his friend Pipo in a speeding truck. Panicked, Ruben ran a red light at high speed and plowed violently into another car. Years later, after Nestor was shot dead attempting a bank robbery, Ruben stood beside his brother’s open grave and made one last offer to Alma. She looked at him and refused.

Before the collision, model Celine Vaz had moved into a flat with a floor-to-ceiling window facing her own giant billboard. Her lover, Hector, had walked out on his wife and daughters at a birthday party to build a new life with her. When Ruben’s truck took out the side of her car at the junction, Celine woke in a hospital ward with her leg held together by steel pins. Her small lapdog, Chispa, had been left behind in the new flat. The dog had fallen through a gap in the floorboards and could not get out. As Chispa’s whines echoed beneath the rooms, Hector tore up the floorboards one by one with a crowbar, while Celine's injured leg turned dark with gangrene. Surgeons amputated her leg above the knee. That same week, workers stripped down the billboard opposite her window, leaving Celine and Hector sitting in the destroyed apartment, gazing at a blank frame.

Cardo, a former guerrilla turned vagrant contract killer, was standing at the junction when Ruben crashed. As smoke rose from the wreckage, Cardo dragged the bleeding rottweiler from the back seat and disappeared into the city. Cardo nursed Tigre back to health in a yard full of strays, feeding the beast by hand. Shortly after watching his estranged wife’s burial from a distance and silently following his grown daughter, Perla, to her apartment building, Cardo returned home to find Tigre had slaughtered every other stray in the yard. Cardo pressed a pistol to the dog's head, held it there, but sat on the ground and found he could not pull the trigger.

Meanwhile, a businessman named Elian paid Cardo half in advance to murder his half-brother and business partner, Sergio. Instead of executing the hit, Cardo abducted Sergio off a pavement and chained him to a bed frame in his empty yard. He then brought Elian face to face with Sergio, placed a loaded pistol on the floor between them, and walked away having taken money from both.

Entering Perla’s flat while she was at work, Cardo sat on her bed and recorded a long confession on her answering machine—explaining who he was, where he went, and why—before taking her photograph from the shelf. Shaved and dressed in clean, ill-fitting clothes, Cardo left all his money on Perla's table. Taking Tigre with him, he walked out into the flat grey wasteland at the edge of the city.

Nadir stood at the counter while his grown daughter, Sahar, translated, enduring the gun dealer’s mocking imitation of his foreign accent before walking out armed with a new pistol. That same night, outside a restaurant, young Trey and Kwame drew guns and carjacked the prosecutor Halstead and his wife Paula. Miles away on a dark road, Officer Boyle pulled over Clay and Renee Hobart for no real reason, forcing Renee against the bonnet and groping her while Clay stood three feet away, paralyzed and silent.

The next morning, Boyle’s partner, Voss, went to their commander and lied about flatulence just to be reassigned away from a racist.

Months later on a rain-slicked country road, Voss would pull over to pick up a young man hitchhiking. When the boy reached into his coat pocket for a cigarette, Voss’s hand would react on instinct, firing two hollow-points into his chest, hauling the body to a ditch, and setting the car ablaze.

Meanwhile, the locksmith Mateo changed the locks on the Halsteads’ house, forced to endure Paula loudly telling her husband that the tattooed man would sell their keys to gang members by morning. Mateo went straight to Nadir’s shop to replace a broken latch, warning the shopkeeper that the entire door frame was rotted and insecure. Convinced Mateo was running an extended con, Nadir spat on the floor and ordered him out.

Desperate for help, Officer Boyle sat across a desk from health insurance clerk Delia Frank, pleading for a referral for his ailing father who wept from pain; Delia offered a flat refusal, leaving Boyle consumed with helpless rage. That night, Nadir’s shop was smashed open along its rotten frame and looted clean. The insurance company refused his claim, citing his failure to repair the warned door.

A week later, Renee Hobart found herself pinned upside down in a burning rollover wreck. Crawling through shattered glass beneath leaking petrol, it was Boyle who dragged her clear. 

Elsewhere, Trey and Kwame sped through the city in Halstead’s stolen car, striking a small shopkeeper named Pham before dumping his battered body outside an emergency room entrance.

When police spotted Clay Hobart driving his own car—erroneously flagged as stolen—four officers held him at gunpoint. Clay stepped out, bellowing in furious indignation, but Voss walked calmly into the crossfire and talked his fellow officers down. Trembling with adrenaline, Clay sped away from the scene with Trey—who had slipped into his passenger seat during the chaos—before pulling over on a dark shoulder and dumping the young man onto the verge without a word.

Consuming himself with fury over his ruined business, Nadir stalked Mateo’s home. When Mateo stepped onto his porch, Nadir raised his handgun and pulled the trigger just as Mateo’s little daughter, Rosie, sprinted into her father's arms. The gun clicked harmlessly; Sahar had secretly bought a box of blanks, saving them both. Nadir fell to his knees, convinced the child was an angel sent to preserve his soul.

Later, Voss picked up Kwame hitchhiking along a rain-slicked road. Misinterpreting Kwame’s reach into his pocket, Voss shot him dead, dumped him in a ditch, and burned his patrol car. Detective Isaiah Reece was called to the roadside scene days later, recognizing the shoes on the charred body as his brother’s. When Reece delivered the news, his mother collapsed on the kitchen floor, weeping and blaming him for never once searching for his missing brother.

Back in her empty house, Paula Halstead tumbled down her grand staircase. Lying injured at the bottom, she wept to her housekeeper Alba, acknowledging that Alba was the only true friend she had left. 

Abandoned on the roadside, Trey bought Pham’s abandoned van at an auction. Opening the cargo doors expecting stolen goods, he discovered two dozen trafficked migrants huddled in the dark. Trey drove them straight to the docks, gave them all his cash, and watched them melt into the night.

As the season’s first snow began to fall, two cars collided at a busy intersection. Both drivers slammed their doors and began screaming at each other before either had even inspected the dented chrome.

All night long, low-flying helicopters droned over every neighborhood, spraying chemical poison against crop pests onto roofs, lawns, and laundry lines across the city. 

By morning, Doctor Neil Hartigan and his painter wife, Bess, began preparing for an evening dinner party, tension simmering between them as Neil changed his shirt twice and Bess put finishing touches on an unfinished canvas. 

Across town, the baker Otto Kemp took an order for a chocolate birthday cake for a young boy named Charlie Rill, noting the collection date on a small card. 

Shortly after, on his way to school, young Charlie was knocked down by a car driven by Rhona, a waitress hurrying to her shift; though shaken, the boy insisted he was completely fine, refused a lift, and walked home alone. 

By afternoon, Charlie collapsed into a deep coma on the living room sofa, forcing his stunned parents, Grant and Elaine, into a desperate vigil beside a hospital ventilator. 

In the sterile corridor, Grant’s estranged father Duff unexpectedly turned up, awkwardly confessing a long-buried affair from decades past to break the heavy silence. 

Left with an uncollected cake and unpaid bill, Otto grew bitter and started making anonymous, menacing phone calls to the Rill house in the dead of night. 

In another home, telephone-sex worker Cheryl folded laundry while whispering fantasies to paying callers, while her husband Stu sat three feet away, seething with quiet fury. 

Escape came when Stu and three friends drove into the mountains for a fishing trip, only to spot the pale body of a young woman floating face down in the shallows. 

Unwilling to ruin their weekend, the men tethered the corpse to the riverbank with fishing line and carried on fishing for two more days before telling authorities. 

When Vern finally returned home and recounted the story, his wife Iris, taking off her party-clown makeup at the kitchen table, was filled with utter disgust at what the men had tolerated. 

Every night, singer Vida performed standards in a dimly lit club, while her cellist daughter, Bee, practiced alone in a silent house. 

Meanwhile, Officer Rowe, secretly cheating on his wife Peg with a woman named Nan, drove the family dog far out of the valley and abandoned it to cover up one of his lies. 

Nan’s ex-husband Cass, the helicopter pilot, learned of her new lover and spent an afternoon sawing every piece of her furniture into wooden splinters. 

While house-sitting for the Hartigans, Ike and Dot amused themselves in the empty house by photographing Dot made up with pale cosmetics as a bruised corpse lying in the hall. 

At the Hartigans' dinner party, Bess casually admitted to an old nude modeling session and an affair, causing Neil to put his glass down with terrifying precision and make a scene before their guests. 

The next morning, Charlie passed away in the hospital; driven to their limit, Grant and Elaine confronted Otto at the bakery, but the old baker broke into tears, fed them warm bread, and grieved with the broken parents. 

That evening, Bee returned home to find Vida asleep in her chair as usual; she walked out to the garage, closed the heavy door, and died as the car engine ran in the dark. 

The following afternoon during a picnic in the hills, Stu’s pent-up rage finally snapped, and he smashed a young woman's head with a heavy rock. 

Shortly after, a sharp tremor shook the entire city, and by nightfall, every death, wreck, and tragedy from the week was folded into a single three-minute bulletin on the evening news.

Above the street, an old man leaned against the frame of an open window, explaining to a younger man that nothing anyone did ever survived time—and that this was not a bitter complaint, but merely a plain, inescapable fact of the world.

Directly below that window, blue light strobed across the asphalt as police officers dragged two men out of a basement club. One shouted furiously into the cool night while the other remained entirely silent, their wrists bound tightly in steel behind their backs.

Inside the reeking dark of the club moments earlier, Jonah had swung a heavy red fire extinguisher into a man's face, bringing it down again and again long after the body had stopped moving. A few feet away, standing quietly among the horrified crowd, the Adder watched the violent mistake unfold, entirely untouched.

Before the heavy cylinder fell, Cort had hunted through the shadows of the room, dragging faces into the dim light until he picked one. But the man he seized caught Cort’s arm at the elbow, turning it with brutal levering force until the bone snapped violently apart.

Earlier, two touts had detached themselves from a side-street doorway, offering for a handful of money to sell the rapist’s name and location. They had pointed Cort and Jonah further down the pavement, steering them directly toward the dark basement entrance of the Pit.

Before the side street, Cort and Jonah had stumbled out of a flat party still half-laughing, only to freeze on the pavement. An ambulance sat idling at the curb, its blue light washing over a trolley, a folded blanket, and a bloodied face resting beneath it that both men recognized instantly.

In the concrete underpass hours before that, the Adder had turned his violence upon Lise, raping her without hurry and cracking her head repeatedly against the tiled floor. At the far end of the tunnel, a passer-by had looked down the length of concrete, hesitated, and slowly backed away into the dark.

Lise had taken those underpass stairs only to avoid crossing four lanes of blinding, relentless headlights. Halfway down the tiled passage, she had walked directly into the shadows where a pimp known as the Adder held a transsexual woman by her hair, explaining something to her with his fist.

She had been completely alone when she descended those stairs, having gathered her coat and left the crowded party without a word. She had spent an hour watching Cort drink past the point of any fun, watching him begin to work the room and pursue other women until disgust finally drove her out the door.

Earlier that evening, the three of them had stood together in the swaying carriage of an underground train. Cort, Jonah, and Lise had argued cheerfully about sex and how much Cort had already had to drink—the easy, effortless argument of people who fully expected to be arguing again tomorrow.

Before the train ride, the afternoon had been untouched, warm, and entirely safe. Lise had laid on her side in the public park while sprinklers turned over cut grass and children ran through the spray, one hand resting flat against her stomach over a book she was not really reading.

Earlier still, she had sat on the porcelain edge of the bathtub, alone in the flat. Holding the small plastic test stick in both hands, she had let herself smile at the positive result before she had told anyone at all.

And in the soft morning light through the thin bedroom curtains, Lise had lay in bed beside Cort, describing a recurring dream of a dark red tunnel she kept walking into, while the two of them traded lazy, affectionate insults about Jonah, her ex-boyfriend who was now only a friend.

A few feet away, standing quietly among the horrified crowd, the Adder watched the violent mistake unfold, entirely untouched.

At the far end of the tunnel, a passer-by had looked down the length of concrete, hesitated, and slowly backed away into the dark.

She had been completely alone when she descended those stairs, having gathered her coat and left the crowded party without a word. She had spent an hour watching Cort drink past the point of any fun, watching him begin to work the room and pursue other women until disgust finally drove her out the door.

And in the soft morning light through the thin bedroom curtains, Lise had lay in bed beside Cort, describing a recurring dream of a dark red tunnel she kept walking into, while the two of them traded lazy, affectionate insults about Jonah, her ex-boyfriend who was now only a friend.

Emlyn sat in Wilder’s drawing room, swirling his glass without drinking. He said he had known about the affair for four years, ever since his wife confessed during their trip abroad. He added softly that he had never thought much of Wilder’s prose in those letters either.

An hour earlier, Wilder had telephoned Emlyn in a state of total agitation, begging him to come over immediately. The call had been frantic, driven by a sudden, sickening realization that his understanding of the past four years was entirely mistaken.

Before the phone call, in a dimly lit bar, Odile had casually let slip a stray detail: Emlyn had spent months publishing a novelist whom Wilder represented—a hack both men secretly despised. It was a professional arrangement conducted entirely outside Odile’s awareness, binding the two men in a quiet, continuing circuit.

Earlier that same afternoon in the bar, two years after they had surrendered their secret meeting place, Odile had sat across from Wilder to give him her news. She announced that her marriage was finally over, explaining that she had spent the previous night confessing every detail of the affair to Emlyn.

Long before that afternoon in the bar, they had stood together in their quiet apartment, dividing up the remaining crockery. The rented rooms had gradually become an oppressive chore rather than a sanctuary, and so they split the plates, packed the linens, and surrendered the lease.

Before the lease was given up, dinner at the married couple’s house had belonged entirely to the men. Sitting across the table, Emlyn and Wilder had bantered endlessly about racquet games and schoolboy sports, trading old memories until Odile had no part in the conversation at all.

Months before that dinner, Emlyn had taken Wilder out for a long, heavy restaurant lunch. Emlyn drank through the afternoon, sharp and persistent as he baited his friend about contemporary fiction, mocking his literary judgment while never once mentioning what he had learned.

Before that lunch, Odile had returned to the rented flat straight from her holiday, unlatching the door and saying nothing whatever about the trip abroad. She let the peaceful afternoon pass exactly like all the others, keeping her husband's reaction entirely to herself.

In the hotel abroad, she had broken down and confessed the truth. Emlyn had listened to her admission without raising his voice, merely remarking that he had always been far fonder of his friend than he was of his wife.

Only hours prior in that foreign hotel lobby, Emlyn had stopped at the desk and pointed to an envelope holding a message held for her. He had asked about it calmly, noting that he recognized the handwriting on the envelope.

Back before the trip, inside the quiet rooms, Odile had told Wilder she was carrying her husband’s child. They had discussed it quietly and decided the news changed nothing about their private household; the rented rooms would go on exactly as before.

Before the pregnancy, they had scouted the quiet district together, taking the lease on the small flat. They filled the cupboards with fresh linens and porcelain plates, deliberately giving their secret an order and a domestic life of its own.

And at the very beginning, during a crowded party downstairs in his closest friend’s house, Wilder had taken Odile by the hand and led her up the dark staircase to an empty room, telling her how lovely she was while the other guests drank below.

Disguised in the flowing robes of devout pilgrims, Solly Two Coats and his crew slipped through security at a northern port diamond house, walking out into the fog with a massive, unblemished stone. Across the sea, his cousin Marv phoned immediately, commanding Solly to bring the payload straight over without delay. But Solly hesitated in the city underworld, where Grigor the Nail told him about a high-stakes bookmaker’s shop. Simultaneously, Grigor secretly tipped off two pawnbrokers, Ike and Benno, urging them to ambush Solly at the bookmaker's to rob him blind.

At the same time, boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their contract fighter, Pretty Sam, to buy a caravan from a camp of local travellers. The encounter turned violent when Finn, a formidable bare-knuckle fighter among the travellers, knocked Sam unconscious over the deal. Suddenly left without a man for gang boss Coldstone’s heavily rigged bout, Halloway was forced to pitch Finn into the match instead, promising Coldstone that Finn would dutifully go down in the fourth round.

Upon arriving in the city, Solly discreetly handed the real diamond over to Hersch, a trusted fence, carrying only a locked, empty briefcase as he headed to the bookmaker's to lay his bet. There, Ike, Benno, and their accomplice Tulley bungled the robbery in a frenzy, seizing Solly’s arm and his briefcase before a furious Grigor chased them off. That night, Finn defied orders in the ring, knocking his opponent out cold in the very first round. Coldstone lost a massive fortune on the broken fix and viciously punished Halloway for the failure.

Overseas investor Marv flew into town, discovered Solly had vanished, and hired a merciless bounty hunter named Ledge to find him. Meanwhile, Grigor trapped Solly in an underworld workshop and severed his arm to open the briefcase lock, only to discover the stone was missing. Ike and Benno had managed to reclaim the stone from Hersch in the interim, but Ledge quickly traced the pawnbrokers, shot their getaway car to pieces, and dragged both the men and the recovered diamond into his possession.

Coldstone took the armless Solly to his farm, fed him to his pigs, and warned Halloway and Digby what fate awaited them if the scheduled rematch went wrong. Halloway and Digby frantically instructed Finn to go down in the fourth round as agreed, but Coldstone’s ruthless henchmen tried to guarantee compliance by setting fire to the travellers' camp, burning Finn’s mother to death inside her caravan.

On a quiet city road, Grigor ambushed Ledge’s vehicle with Ike and Benno trapped inside. The chaotic shootout ended in mutual destruction, leaving Ledge, Grigor, and Benno dead on the pavement. Amidst the carnage, Tulley quietly slipped away into the shadows, taking with him a dog that had swallowed the loose diamond off the floorboard during the chaos.

At the rematch, Finn bided his time until the fourth round arrived, then unleashed a terrifying blow that knocked his opponent out cold once more. Simultaneously, vengeful travellers drew weapons throughout the crowd, launching a coordinated massacre against Coldstone’s unsuspecting henchmen. With the gang boss stripped of his guard, Halloway and Digby tracked Coldstone down to his private room and shot him dead. By morning, the travellers had vanished into the mist.

Days later, the stray dog was handed in at a pet shop, where it coughed up the swallowed diamond onto the counter. Halloway and Digby, who had come in for a mundane errand, picked up the stone, completely astonished to hold the priceless treasure that had destroyed everyone else.
